title: Refried Beans
subtitle: Creamy mashed pinto beans fried with garlic and cumin
excerpt: Pinto beans cooked with garlic and cumin, then mashed and fried in oil until creamy and rich. The essential Tex-Mex side dish and the base layer of nachos and seven-layer dip.
sourceNotes: Refried beans (frijoles refritos): a Mexican and Tex-Mex staple made from mashed and fried beans, most commonly pinto beans in northern Mexico and Tex-Mex cooking. The name is a translation error from the Spanish; 'refritos' means 'well-fried', not 'fried again'. Based on classic Mexican and American Tex-Mex published sources.

recipe.freezeNotes: Freeze in portions for up to 3 months. Defrost in the fridge overnight and reheat in a pan with a splash of water.
recipe.batchNotes: Double or triple the batch; freezes perfectly.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Make ahead and refrigerate for up to 4 days. Reheat in a pan with a little water or stock.

content.text: Refried beans are pinto beans cooked with aromatics until soft, then mashed and fried. The name frijoles refritos means 'well-fried', not 'fried again'. Tinned pinto beans make this a 15-minute dish without compromising on quality. The beans need to cook in the oil long enough to dry out slightly and absorb the garlic and cumin; rushed refried beans taste of raw fat. The texture should be smooth and creamy enough to spread, not stiff.

items.prepNote: two tins, drained and rinsed — reserve 150 ml of the liquid

content.text: Heat {{vegetable-oil}} of oil in a wide frying pan over medium heat. Cook {{onion}} of finely chopped onion for 5 minutes until soft. Add {{garlic}} of crushed garlic, the cumin, and chilli powder. Cook for 2 minutes.
Add the drained pinto beans. Cook for 2-3 minutes, stirring, so the beans absorb the oil and start to break down at the edges.

Mash roughly with a potato masher or fork, adding splashes of the reserved bean liquid as you go until the texture is smooth enough to spread, somewhere between hummus and mashed potato. Season generously with salt and the lime juice.
Cook for a further 3-4 minutes, stirring regularly. The beans should begin to pull away from the sides of the pan as they fry. Adjust consistency with more liquid if needed.

items.symptom: Beans are too stiff and paste-like
items.cause: Not enough liquid added while mashing
items.fix: Add reserved bean liquid (or warm water) a tablespoon at a time while mashing until the consistency loosens. The beans thicken as they cool, so cook them slightly looser than you want to serve them.

items.cause: Not cooked in the oil long enough, or too much oil
items.fix: Cook the beans in the oil for at least 3-4 minutes after mashing; this lets the beans absorb the oil and lose the raw-fat taste. If still greasy, add a splash of water and cook off.

items.symptom: Beans stick and burn in the pan
items.cause: Heat too high or not enough oil
items.fix: Keep the heat at medium. Add another splash of oil or bean liquid if the pan looks dry. Stir regularly during the frying stage.

items.cause: Under-salted or spices not cooked in
items.fix: Season generously with salt; beans need more than you think. Add the spices before the beans so they cook in the oil first. A squeeze of lime at the end is essential.

content.text: Refried beans are one of the defining dishes of northern Mexican and Tex-Mex cooking. Pinto beans are the traditional variety in these regions; black beans are more common in southern Mexico and Central America. The word 'refried' is a mistranslation of frijoles refritos, which means well-fried or thoroughly fried. The beans are cooked in fat once, not twice. They appear as a side dish, a burrito filling, a base for nachos, and the bottom layer of seven-layer dip.
